hotspot_comment: Land preparation and the planting of cereal crops, primarily maize, have begun in parts of Angola. However, a slight delay in the start of the season has been observed across central regions. According to [https://fews.net/southern-africa/angola/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), this delay is likely driven by a forecast El Niño-induced late onset of the rainy season alongside severe national fertilizer shortages, which have prompted even better-off farmers to delay and scale back land preparation. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 points to a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions, particularly across central and southern areas. Conversely, only the interior northeastern provinces are projected to receive near-average to slightly above-average precipitation. As reported by [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=AGO] FAO GIEWS (03/09), this dry outlook is heavily influenced by the ongoing El Niño event that emerged in June, which is historically associated with suppressed rainfall totals across much of Southern Africa. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

Planting of Season A crops, including beans, maize and sorghum, is underway. Rainfall has been average over the past three dekads, but biomass remains below average across the country, with 71% of cropland in Cankuzo, 75% in Muyinga and 74% in Ruyigi showing poor vegetation conditions. Linked to the ongoing El Niño, [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Copernicus seasonal forecasts point to wetter-than-usual conditions in the coming months. According to [https://fews.net/east-africa/burundi/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET, the Northern Lowlands are expected to deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) during the October–January lean season following consecutive below-average harvests in 2026, while fuel shortages, the closed border with Rwanda and staple prices 10–50% above the five-year average continue to constrain food access. Season A production is also expected to be below average due to fertilizer shortages and the delayed onset of rains, and strong El Niño-related rainfall is likely to cause flooding, landslides and localized crop losses.
Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

Long-rains harvesting in unimodal areas is nearing completion, with reduced production following prolonged dry spells and rainfall deficits during critical crop-development stages. The North Rift and parts of western and central Kenya remain particularly affected. FEWS NET estimates long-rains maize production at 22–28% below the five-year average nationally, with a shortfall of approximately 43% in the North Rift. Short-rains planting is under way in most bimodal areas, although dry conditions were observed in some areas during the second dekad of October. Rainfall forecasts for the remainder of the short rains season point towards above average rains which will be critical in crop development, pasture and water availability. It is important however to bear in mind that high intensity rainfall will not be immediately beneficial to drought affected crop areas and that there is a high risk of adverse impacts including increased risk of flooding.

Planting of summer cereal crops began in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. Despite this forecast poor start to the rainy season, reports from [https://fews.net/southern-africa/lesotho/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026) note that heavily subsidized government inputs and favourable soil moisture from recent rains are expected to support average overall planted areas. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

In Madagascar, the 2025-2026 season has started in October with cereals and legumes planting in the Grand South (Anosy, Androy and Atsimo Andrefana) under close to average moisture conditions. In the centre and north, rice planting should start in November or December under drier than average rainfall conditions, which are expected to persist through March, according to the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast. The Grand South is estimated to have about 2 million people facing acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 and above) as a result of poor harvests due to cyclones or previous droughts (2020, 2021 and 2022) and poor socio economic conditions including rising food prices and fewer agricultural jobs according to [https://www.wfp.org/countries/madagascar] WFP.

Land preparation for the 2026/27 cereal cropping season has started. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions across central and southern parts of the country and average conditions in the north. This grim outlook aligns with [https://fews.net/southern-africa/malawi/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), which reports that a strengthening El Niño persisting through February 2027 is expected to drive erratic, below-average rainfall across central and southern Malawi, disrupting land preparation, crop establishment, and overall agricultural production. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

Planting of summer cereal crops in main northern producing provinces is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

Planting of Season A crops, including beans, maize and sorghum, is nearly complete. Rainfall has been average over the past three dekads, but biomass remains below average across the country, with 69% of cropland in Iburasirazuba (Eastern Province) and 83% in Kigali showing poor vegetation conditions. Linked to the ongoing El Niño, [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Copernicus seasonal forecasts point to wetter-than-usual conditions in the coming months. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/rwanda/wfp-rwanda-country-brief-october-2026] WFP, the average cost of the food basket in Rwanda rose by 3% month-on-month and 7% year-on-year in September 2026, as food inflation and high fuel and transport costs offset the benefits of recent harvests. Refugee households have been hit particularly hard, with funding shortfalls limiting assistance to 50% of planned entitlements, while contingency planning for floods and landslides has been stepped up ahead of El Niño-driven above-average rainfall.

Maize is being planted in bimodal areas for the Vuli season, while planting of Msimu maize and sorghum is approaching in unimodal areas. Although most of the country is still off-season, biomass is below average in parts of the west and north, with 75% of cropland in Katavi, 81% in Kigoma and 60% in Mara showing poor vegetation status. Linked to the ongoing El Niño, [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Copernicus seasonal forecasts point to wetter-than-usual conditions in the coming months. According to the Tanzania Meteorological Authority (TMA), conditions are already turning wetter, with rainfall on 22–23 October exceeding October monthly averages at some stations, and the heaviest rains expected between November 2026 and January 2027 ([https://thechanzo.com/2026/10/26/tma-extends-el-nino-alert-to-western-and-southern-tanzania-as-november-rains-near] The Chanzo). While this could support Vuli crop development, very strong El Niño conditions combined with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole also raise the risk of flooding, crop losses and transport disruptions ([https://www.thecitizen.co.tz/tanzania/news/national/tanzania-braces-for-heavy-rains-as-el-ni%C3%B1o-raises-flood-risks-5642818] The Citizen).

First-season crops were harvested under predominantly average or favourable conditions, although localized production losses occurred. In Karamoja, below-average and poorly distributed rainfall constrained the unimodal crop, particularly in Kotido. Second-season planting is under way following a delayed and dry start in several bimodal areas. Forecast above-normal October–December rainfall could improve crop establishment and soil moisture, although flooding and waterlogging remain concerns. High food prices, localised harvest shortfalls and pressure on refugee-hosting areas continue to increase humanitarian needs. The IPC analysis covering July 2026–January 2027 estimates approximately 3.6 million people in Crisis or worse, a 6% increase compared with 2025.

Planting of summer cereal crops is set to begin at the end of October. However, an initial delay in the start of the season has been observed across western and northern areas, specifically affecting the Western, North-Western, Copperbelt, and Northern provinces. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of severe, drier-than-normal conditions across central and southern Zambia, contrasting with expected normal to wetter-than-average conditions in the far northern provinces. This grim outlook aligns with [https://fews.net/southern-africa/zambia/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026) reports that warn of a very strong El Niño bringing erratic, below-average rainfall and a delayed onset to southern and western Zambia, with prolonged dry spells during the critical December–February period expected to heavily constrain planting, crop growth, and agricultural labor income. Given these compounding factors, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

This grim outlook aligns with reports from [https://fews.net/southern-africa/zimbabwe/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), which predict below-average rainfall and high temperatures driven by El Niño. In response, the government has approved a comprehensive six-pillar mitigation plan focused on food security, agricultural support, and financial relief ([https://farmfutureafrica.co.zw/zimbabwes-six-pillar-super-el-nino-strategy-what-farmers-need-to-know/] Farm Future Africa). Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.
